newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's coffee inventories spark quality debate.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's coffee inventories spark quality debate.

text.p: The National Coffee Growers' Federation has offered private exporters 300,000 70-kg bags from its stockpiles to help ease the country's tight supply situation.
But the old coffee being offered from federation inventories may not live up to the high standards long associated with the country's supply.
One private firm, Compania Cafetera Agricola de Santander, examined 190,000 bags of the coffee being offered from federation-controlled Almacafe warehouses in the cities of Buga, Cartago and Aremnia.
The study found that 21 percent of the coffee was damaged by the plague known as "broca" that has infected roughly half of Colombia's coffee plantations.

It also said the coffee had a higher-than-average humidity content that would tend to give it a stronger taste than export-quality excelso. Furthermore, 17 percent of the beans were found to be of inferior quality or abnormal in shape and size. Usually, only 5.2 percent of coffee in any lot is classified as something less than optimum in terms of quality.

"It's true, the coffee that the federation has (in inventory) definitely does not match the quality of fresh coffee. But that doesn't mean that it's no good," said one private roaster who asked not to be identified by name.

He said the coffee, from harvests in 1994-95, had specific target markets like Spain and Italy where consumers are less inclined to object to the strong taste that comes from additional roasting time.

"The problem is with more demanding markets like Germany or the Scandinavian countries," he said, adding that the coffee would obviously sell at a discount and well below the premium price that fresh excelso fetches on world markets .

The federation has authorized private exporters to ship 1.07 million 70-kg bags of fresh coffee between April and June. It authorized shipment of up to 300,000 bags of old coffee during the same time period.
A federation source said 100,000 bags of the old coffee had already been sold to exporters, although he was unable to specify when and where they were sold abroad.
"It's a coffee that's very well received in the United States and Europe ... there have been no complaints from clients."

Industry sources said last month that the federation, which is short of fresh coffee to meet its own export commitments, had asked private exporters to swap 600,000 bags of fresh coffee for 800,000 bags of "oldish" beans from its stockpiles.
Exporters said no such deal had been agreed, however, and many note that their contracts with roasters abroad specify that they are only permitted to ship fresh coffee.
"I have no use for old coffee at all," said one exporter.
Colombia's supply problems are expected to ease in April when the so-called Mitaca harvest, which provides about 40 percent of the country's total production, will get fully under way.
